# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

screens.why5: The generic line "Would you try this for real?" keeps the intent but drops the step I typed, ordering a pair with free returns, so an email sign-up stands in for a real order.
screens.instead: Ask people who say yes to order a pair with free returns? Hint: People who say yes get a line at the end: "Would you order a pair with free returns? Leave your email." You see who said yes on the Pilot tab. Options: Yes, ask them / No, don't ask

screens.why1: Choosing who asks the questions is an obvious last step before the study goes out to deaf and hard-of-hearing adults, and no earlier screen asked it.
screens.why2: The question is plain and the hint clearly explains the video, the written questions, the 400 credits and the text-message link, though it is a lot to read at once.
screens.why3: I know my customers, but a 5-second voice sample tells me little about what matters to them, such as whether the interviewer's face is easy to lipread, so I would partly be guessing.
screens.why4: The two names are distinct and Daphne is sensibly preselected, but a 'Hear' sample is the wrong thing to compare for deaf people and there is no written-only option for those who don't want a speaking video.
screens.why5: It keeps my 'deaf or hard-of-hearing adults' wording and accounts for them with written questions and typing or tapping, so nothing I typed has changed.
screens.instead: Who should appear on video for deaf or hard-of-hearing adults? Compare each interviewer's face and captions, not only their voice: Daphne (watch a 5 s sample) / Saskia (watch a 5 s sample) / No video, written questions only.

screens.why1: Once I've settled who asks my questions, the next obvious thing to decide before sending is how my deaf and hard-of-hearing respondents will take the interview.
screens.why2: The choice is plain, but I had to read "Still recording · ready in a few minutes" and "Ready when Daphne is" twice to see that they mean Daphne's video is still being made.
screens.why3: I know how my people handle a talking video and a text screen, because captions and phones are my whole business, so I can answer this from what I know.
screens.why4: My true answer, Read and tap, is there and the three options are distinct, but Daphne is described in terms of hearing ("aloud", "Hear her", catching speech in a loud room) with nothing on whether her video suits deaf people or those who don't speak.
screens.why5: It keeps my "deaf or hard-of-hearing adults" exactly as I typed it and doesn't change what my study means.
screens.instead: How should deaf or hard-of-hearing adults answer? Read and tap: they read each question and tap or type, no sound needed (ready now). AI interviewer Daphne: she speaks on video with every question written on screen, and they answer by talking, typing or tapping (her video is ready in a few minutes). Let them choose: they pick either one when they open the link (ready once her video is).

screens.why1: Once I've chosen how people answer and the study is ready to send, who receives a link is the obvious next and last decision.
screens.why2: The three choices read plainly on first pass, and I know at once whether I mean people I can name, a search list or a community post.
screens.why3: I know who I can reach, from deaf and hard-of-hearing people I already know to the groups they gather in, so I can answer from my own situation.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover the ways I'd reach people, but 'Contacts page' names a part of Keel I haven't seen in this flow, so that option is slightly odd at first read.
screens.why5: The screen is about distribution, changes nothing I typed about AirCaps, and my pick of people I know by name is kept as the first option.

screens.why1: As the first screen it plainly checks whether I'm someone this study is for, and I can see why they'd ask before anything else.
screens.why2: Hearing people is how I'd talk about it myself, and I get the question straight away.
screens.why3: I know whether I talk with hearing people in a week, because I do it at the shops, at work and with family.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, they don't overlap, and no escape is needed on a simple screener about my week.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product, a company or any founder's language reaches me, only a question about my week.
screens.why6: Said aloud it is one short question I can answer yes or no on one hearing, though the words *yes or no* aren't spoken, as the record shows only the stem.

screens.why1: After being asked whether I talk with hearing people every week, showing me an idea about following those conversations makes obvious sense, and the kicker tells me it is an idea to consider.
screens.why2: Captions, glasses, app, lens and eye contact are all words I use and understand on first reading.
screens.why3: I know what it is to lose a conversation while looking away to read or lip-read, so I can picture this from my own life.
screens.why4: This is a card to read, with no options, rows, chips or value box.
screens.why5: The product is shown on purpose as an Imagine card in plain words, with the belief clearly marked as the builders', and no role labels or founder terms reach me.
screens.why6: It is five short sentences with no parenthesis, slash or abbreviation, so it says well in one go, and only the repeated mention of captions and lens is slightly redundant.

screens.why1: After being asked if I talk with hearing people and shown the idea, it makes sense to ask how much I lose out in those conversations today.
screens.why2: The words are simple, but 'miss' needs a second read because I might miss part of a conversation, most of it, or stay out of it altogether.
screens.why3: Missing conversations is my daily life, but nobody keeps a monthly count, so I would be guessing at a number.
screens.why4: The number box, 'None' and 'I can't recall' fit, but 'I'd rather not say' is a second escape that adds nothing, since not recalling already gives me a way out.
screens.why5: Nothing of the founder's product or terms reaches me here; 'conversations' and 'miss' are ordinary words for my situation.
screens.why6: The question says well, but 'A number of conversations last month, or a low and a high; none is 0' is a clumsy instruction to hear, and it drops the on-screen 'I'd rather not say'.
screens.instead: Think of the last week: about how many conversations with hearing people did you lose track of because they were too fast or too noisy? Type a number, or choose None or I can't recall.

screens.why1: Asking what it's worth makes sense straight after the glasses idea, but the heading says 'What you do today' and this isn't about my day, so it comes a bit abruptly.
screens.why2: 'Worth to you up front' and then 'a month' is how I'd talk about hearing aids and their plans, so I understand it on first reading.
screens.why3: I've paid for hearing kit and know what that costs, but I've never bought captioning glasses or seen them work, so my figure would be partly a guess.
screens.why4: The bands are complete and don't overlap, and 'I wouldn't pay' and 'I can't say' both fit, but $599 looks odd beside the round numbers.
screens.why5: The name on the idea card is there on purpose, but the odd $599 edge looks like somebody's real price showing through, which nudges my answer.
screens.why6: The two steps are short and easy to hold, but 'Or say you can't say' trips when spoken, and as someone hard of hearing I could easily mishear close spoken figures like $50 and $15.
screens.instead: What would AirCaps be worth to you up front? Under $250; $250 to under $600; $600 to under $1,000; $1,000 to under $2,500; $2,500 or more; or I wouldn't pay for this. Or: I can't say.

screens.why1: I just gave a price, so being asked what would make it worth more follows straight on from that.
screens.why2: The words are plain and I could answer on first reading or first hearing, because the amount is the band I just picked.
screens.why3: I know what fails me in conversations, like noise, speed and group talk, so I can say what would make it worth more to me.
screens.why4: It is only a box to type in, with no options or chips to judge.
screens.why5: AirCaps is the name from the idea card I was shown on purpose, and nothing new about the product or the founder's terms reaches me here.
screens.why6: It is short and easy to hold, but it is two sentences and the spoken figures $250 to under $599 are a slight mouthful before the question.

screens.why1: Coming right after what AirCaps is worth to me, I can see it is about paying, but who else had to agree is an abrupt turn for a thing I'd buy for myself.
screens.why2: The words are easy, but I have to stop on "something like this" and work out whether it means captioning glasses, a hearing aid, or a captioning app.
screens.why3: I can answer if my hearing aids or a captioning app count, and I may remember a spouse or insurer being involved, but if I've never bought anything like these glasses I'd be guessing what counts.
screens.why4: The yes and no answers are shuffled, and "No, someone else decided for me" fits oddly as an answer to "did anyone else have to agree", while "I can't recall one" only loosely covers never having bought anything like this.
screens.why5: Nothing of the founder's product or terms reaches me here; it doesn't even name AirCaps and only says "something like this".
screens.why6: It is short and can be said, but hearing yes, no, yes, no in that order makes the four hard to hold after one hearing, and "you can't recall one" leaves me unsure what "one" is.
screens.instead: The last time you paid for a hearing aid or captioning device or app, who made the decision? I decided alone; I decided with someone else; someone else decided for me; or I can't recall one.

screens.why1: After asking what it's worth and who has to agree, it makes sense to finish by asking whether I'd actually order a pair.
screens.why2: Ordering a pair of glasses with free returns is everyday language, and I'd understand it on first reading with the card above it.
screens.why3: I can answer this from my own life because I know whether I'd risk an order on captioned glasses if I could send them back, though no price is named.
screens.why4: My true answer is there and the lack of an escape suits a yes-or-no commitment, but 'Probably not' and 'No' sit close together with only a firm yes on the other side.
screens.why5: AirCaps appears only on the idea card shown on purpose, and nothing else of the founder's plan or terms for people reaches me.
screens.why6: It is short with three options I can hold, but said aloud without the card, 'a pair' never says a pair of what, so the glasses have to be remembered from earlier.
screens.instead: If AirCaps glasses were ready today, would you order a pair with free returns, or not? Yes, I'd order a pair; Probably not; No.
